Percentage of armed recruits from Orissa 
*282. MISS FRIDA TOPNO: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the percentage of recruitment in armed forces from Orissa is 
less as compared to other States; 
(b) the number of recruitment centres of Army, Navy and Air Force 
separately in Orissa; and 
(c) the reasons for less recruitment from Orissa and the remedial steps 
proposed for it? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) to 
(c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
The recruitment of Sailors in Navy and Airmen in Air Force is carried out 
on the basis of all-India merit and no specific quota is allotted to any particular 
State. Therefore, no comparison can be drawn with respect to recruitment to 
these forces from different States. 
The recruitment of Jawans in Army is based on allocation of vacancies to 
States. Distribution of 'all -India all class vacancies' of Army among States is 
done on the basis of their Recruitable Male Population (RMP). The RMP is that 
proportion of the male population, which meets the laid down age limits and 
minimum standards of education for enrolment to Army. This is expressed as a 
percentage of the total Male Population (TMP). This method of allocation of 
vacancies among the States/UTs ensures that each State gets its due and 
equitable share of vacancies available in a year in Army. The RMP of Orissa is 
3.66 per cent which is more than that of 21 States/Union Territories. 
As the States have different allocation of vacancies because of variation 
in population, State -wise recruitment to Army generally conforms to the 
allocation profile. 
The position of vacancies allotted to Orissa and the actual intake during 
the last three years was as under:

The above table would show that there are minor shortfalls in the years 
1996-97 and 1997-98 whereas the shortfall in 1998-99 is large. 
The following seem to be the main reasons for shortfall in recruitment to 
Army in Orissa: 
(a) Low success rate in written examination. 
(b) Non-confirmation to the prescribed physical and medical standards. 
The following measures have been taken to improve recruitment in 
Orissa:—  
(i) Wider publicity for recruitment rallies to attract large number of 
youth. 
(ii) Grant of special dispensation in education qualification to Adivasis of 
Orissa from class 10 to class 5 for joining Army as soldier(GD). 
(iii) Directions have been issued that RMP based quota of any State 
should not lapse; if it is not filled in a particular year the backlog 
should be carried forward to the next year.

SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Sir, in the army recruitment, there is no

operates. Sir, in as carry forward of the backlog is concerned, this is an order that

Dialogue with NSCN and ULFA 
*284. SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) die latest position as regards die dialogue with NSCN (IM) and other 
militant organisations; 
(b) the effect of arrest of General Secretary of NSCN (IM) at Bangkok, on 
die dialogue; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to have a dialogue with ULFA? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L. K. ADVANI): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on die Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
(a) The cease-fire between die Government of India and die NSCN (I/M) 
is valid till 31.7.2000. Efforts a re also being made to engage other 
underground outfits in die North-East in a dialogue. 
(b) The Government of India remains committed to die peace process. 
The proposed current round of talks with die NSCN (I/M) has, however, 
been postponed at its request foll owing the arrest of Th. Muivah in 
Thailand. 
(c) The Government is committed to restoration of peace and has extended 
an invitation to all those who have stayed from the paths of togetherness 
to come forward for talks within die four corners of our Constitution. 
The ULFA has, however, not responded for talks so far within the 
parameters indicated. 
SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Sir, the hon. Home Minister, in part (a) of 
his reply, has said that the cease-fire between the Government of India and die 
NSCN (I/M) is valid till 31.7.2000. Efforts are also being made to engage other 
underground outfits in the North-East in a dialogue. But die problem does not 
end there. Sir, I think, there is a. parallel Government which is engaged in 
extortion of money. We have seen that die so-called Government of the People's 
Republic of Nagalim is extorting money from the public off and on. One such 
self-styled captain of an illegal Naga Army ordered the oil tanker drivers who 
collected oil from Khotkhoti Depot situated in Golaghat Distric t of Assam to 
pay money. On 25th January, he ordered every tanker driver to pay him Rs. 500 
per trip for the so -called Naga sovereignty. In the event of their refusal, he 
threatened to take action, as he deemed fit. Cash receipts were also given to

them. It shows that a parallel authority is operating there. They are operating

Secondly, I think the Ministry should, at least, have a dialogue with that

16 

{15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
STATEMENT 
(a) Yes, Sir. The textile account for approximately l/3rd of our total exports. 
(b) In 1997-98, the textile exports grew in dollar terms by 4.2% compared to 1996-
97 while in 1996-97 the same grew by 10.8% compared to 1995-96. 
(c) The main reasons for decline are:—  
(i) Slow growth in cotton yarn exports due to slowdown in South East Asian 
economy. 
(ii) Low unit value realisation in non-restrained items in the case of apparel 
articles. 
(iii) Non-release of exceptional flexibilities in full by EU during 1997. 
(iv) General recession in the world market (there was overall decline in 
Indian exports by 2%). 
(d) Government have been taking several steps from time to time to 
boost textile exports. Some of the important initiatives are as under:— 
(1) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme has been made 
operational with effect from 1 -4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation 
and Upgradation of textile sector. 
(2) The New Export Entitlement (Quote) Policy for the period 2000— 2004 
has been announced to provide stability and continuity and encourage 
competitiveness in textile exports. 
(3) Non-Quota Entitlement (NQE) System for encouraging Non-Quota exports 
to Quota and non-quota countries has been retained* to boost exports 
in apparel sector-value added segment of Indian textiles. 
(4) Threshold limit under the Zero Duty Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) 
Scheme has been reduced to Rs. 1 crore in respect of certain prescribed 
textile machinery. 
(5) Exports of cotton yarn by Export Oriented Unit (EOU)/Export 
Promotion Zone (EPZ)/EPCG units has been liberalised. 
(6) Zero Duty import of certain categories of trimmings & 
embellishments has been allowed.

Purchase of Residential Plots in Himachal Pradesh 
*287. SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Central Government employees are not allowed 
to purchase residential plots in the State of Himachal Pradesh; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether Government would contemplate a policy decision allowing 
the Central Government employees to purchase residential plots in Himachal 
Pradesh; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): (a) to (d) 
According to information received from the Government of Himachal Pradesh, 
section 118 of the Himachal Pradesh Tenancy and Land Reforms Act, 1972 
provides that non- agriculturists cannot purchase land without the permission 
of the State Government for the prescribed purpose. The word agriculturist has 
been defined under section 2 of the said A ct as a person who cultivates land 
personally in an estate situated in Himachal Pradesh. Therefore, a Central 
Government employee, who is an agriculturist under the provisions of the Act, 
can purchase land in his name. However, if he is not an agriculturis t, he can 
purchase land in Himachal Pradesh only with the prior permission of the State 
Government. Besides, a non -agriculturist can purchase land/built up house 
from the Himachal Pradesh State Housing Board and Development Authority 
without the permission of the State Government. A non- agriculturist can also 
purchase land within the Municipal areas without permission in case he was 
residing in Himachal Pradesh on the commencement of the Act, i.e., 21.2.1974.

THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): (a) to (c) No

Government of India and the concerned State Governments continuously review 
the situation arising out of militancy, terrorism,  insurgency and extremist 
activities. 
In order to tackle cross-border terrorism in Jammu & Kashmir, Government 
of India has implemented an action plan. For neutralising militancy/terrorism 
in the North- East various steps including deployment of CPMFs and A rmy, 
improved coordination and intelligence sharing between security forces, 
modernisation/upgradation of State Police Forces etc. have been undertaken. 
For effectively countering Left Wing Extremism, the affected States of 
Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Orissa were requested 
to prepare integrated action plans encompassing the development as well as 
security aspects of the problem for the affected areas. The States have also been 
advised to take vigorous follow -up action. The Governm ent of India has also 
set up a coordination centre headed by the Union Home Secretary with Chief 
Secretaries and Directors General of Police of the States affected by Left Wing 
Extremism, as its members, to review steps taken to check the Left Wing Extremist 
activities, monitor the plan of action in respect of each state etc. 
In addition, in order to minimise attacks due to landmine and/or IED 
blasts on security forces/police personnel/civilians, steps such as deployment 
of road opening parties, use of metal detectors, mine protected vehicles etc. 
are being taken.

India;

contract dated 24.3.1986 was concluded with M/s A.B. Bofors, Sweden for

(SHRI I. D. SWAMI): (a) Yes, Sir.

Governments, Howere, the Central Government has been stressing upon the

Power Crisis in the Ensuing Summer 
2233. DR. MOHAN BABU: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a worst power crisis all over the country is 
anticipated in the ensuing summer; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the action taken by Government to avert the crisis? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Based on the tentative generation target and 
anticipated requirement of energy in various regions of the country during the 
ensuing summer months of April/May and June, 2000, the country is likely to 
face energy shortage of the order of 5.5%. The energy shortage in Northern, 
Southern and Western Regions are likely to be of the order of 7.1 % 6.8% and 
4.4% respectively. Eastern and North -Eastern Regions are not likely  to face 
any energy shortages. 
(b) The reasons for shortage of power are greater increase in requirement 
of energy compared to availability, low voltage conditions in the grid due to 
inadequate installation of shunt capacitors, shortage of peaking power in the  
grid, constraints in transmission and distribution system and low PLF of some 
of the power station. 
(c) In order to improve availability of power and generation capacity and 
make optimal use of the available power resources in the country, the following 
measures have been taken:—  
(i) Expeditious implementation of capacity addition programme. 
(ii) Promotion of measures for demand side management such as flattening 
of load curve by staggering weekly off day of industrial consumers 
and regulation of power supply to consumers through grouping 
restrictions. 
(iii) Renovation and modernisation(R&M) of existing generating stations. 
(iv) Disbursement of loans by Power Finance Corporation for improving 
operation and maintenance of thermal power stations under accelerated 
generation programme. 
(v) Promotion of inter-state and inter-regional power transfers. 
118 

[15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(vi) Coordinated operation of hydro, thermal nuclear and gas turbine power 
stations in the regional power system. 
(vii) Augmentation of transmission, transformation capacity in the power 
system and installation of shunt capacitors to improve the voltage. 
(viii) Reduction of transmission and distribution losses.

Statement-III 
Resolution of the Chief Ministers/Power Ministers Conference Held on 
26.02.2000 
The Power Ministers' Conferen ce took note of the impending difficult 
situation facing the power supply industry in the country due to continuing 
decline in commercial viability of the sector as a whole. It noted the fact that:— 
1. Outstanding dues of CPSUs have been increasing and have now reached 
Rs. 23,000 crores. This trend if maintained would adversely affect 
their current operations apart from their future expansion plans. 
2. Financial closure for private power projects is becoming increasingly 
difficult. 
3. The states are unable to finance new projects on their own. 
4. Increases in budgetary support from state governments as well as central 
government for this sector is not feasible due to fiscal deficits. 
II. The primary factors responsible for this unsustainable financial 
situation are:    
(i) Theft and pilferage at the macro level are estimated to be over Rs. 
20,000 crores per annum. 
(ii) Technical losses in transmission & distribution for the country are 
also too high. 
128 

[ 15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(iii) Large number of the thermal stations in the State sector run at an 
operational efficiency of less than 40%. 
(iv) The average annual operational losses of the State Power Sector for the 
country is over as. 12,000 crores. 
III. It was also recognised that the cross subsidies cannot be sus tained if 
industrial tariffs make Industry non -competitive in the new environment of 
increasing globalisation with elimination of quantitative and other restrictions. It 
becomes necessary to ensure that Indian Industry is not handicapped by 
unsatisfactory power supply or by tariff which makes it non-competitive. Further, the 
consumer, including the fanner has a legitimate claim for uninterrupted good 
quality power supply. His willingness to pay reasonable costs is 
underestimated. 
Resolutions 
1. The Power Mi nisters' resolved after taking into account all the  
problems facing the power sector, that with the intention of achieving 
commercial viability and providing power at reasonable rate to all,  
reform must be undertaken with determination, vigor and a sense o f 
urgency. Delay in reform only increases the financial cost of reforms, 
and the burden of liabilities only increases. Reforms must begin to  
show results within the next 2-3 years. The key elements of the reform 
strategy are:—  
(a) Energy Audit at all levels. 
(b) Time-bound programme of 100% metering of all consumers by 
December 2001. 
(c) Reduction and finally, elimination of power theft within a specified 
time frame. 
(d) Strengthening/upgradation of sub -transmission and distribution 
system by taking sub-station as an unit on a priority basis. 
 
2. If the above appears unattainable in the existing set up corporatisation/ 
cooperatization/privatization of distributions, would have to be 
undertaken. 
3. Since a large number of thermal stations within the State sector are 
running at a P LF below 40% immediate Renovation & Modernisation 
including Life Extension would need to be undertaken on an urgent 
 129 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2000] 
basis. Similarly, R&M/LE would require to be undertaken for old 
hydel power plants on priority. 
4. Effective functioning of State Electricity Regulatory Commissions is 
essential for rationalization of tariff, and balancing the interests of the 
consumer and the need for commercial viability of the utilities in the 
environment where private sector participation in the industry is 
expected to gradually increase. 
5. Unbundling and corporatization of State Electricity Boards/ bench-
marking through separate distribution profit centres/corporations/ 
companies may facilitate the Regulatory Commissions in prom- oting 
competition within the power supply industry —competition being 
the key to lower prices. 
6. It was noted that the power system network in country has an unmatched 
reach to consumers and with the installation of optic fibre cables 
along the existing power lines using its right of way, it has the potential 
of generating very large resources in the coming years by providing 
facilities for multipurpose communication including cable TV, IT 
services, Telecom services, etc. Hence efforts need to be made to 
creatively tap this potential source of large revenue from convergence. 
7. In order to promote reforms, a new draft central legislation which 
obviates the need for separate enactments for the States, is being 
considered. The draft Bill submitted by the NCAER would form the 
basis for a national debate and a consensus on the contents of the new 
Bill. The States would be sending their detailed comments on this 
draft Bill, to the Ministry of Power at the earliest.

Study on India's Power Policies by World Bank 
2244. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the attention of the Government has been drawn to the news 
item captioned ""Government rejects WB study on India's power policies" as  
reported in the Times of India dated 29th December, 1999; 
(b) whether the World Bank is interested to conduct study on India's  
power sector policies; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(d) the details of guidelines issued by the World Bank during the past 
three years with regard to India's power policies; and 
(e) to what extent Government have implemented them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Yes, Sir. The Government is aware of the news item 
which states that the Government rejects World Bank study on India's power 
policies. The Government does not agr ee with the conclusion sought to be 
projected in the document of the World Bank since the entire document is 
based on the basis of some studies conducted in only two states,"viz. Bihar and 
Andhra Pradesh. The per capita emission of carbon-di-oxide in India is between 
one tenth to one twentieth of the per capita carbon -di- oxide emission in 
developed countries. Besides, all power plants in India are established after 
obtaining full environmental clearance. The Government is also committed to 
promoting effici ency. The use of efficient generating plants and pollution 
control technologies is bound to reduce the level of emissions. The efforts of 
energy conservation including demand side management will also reduce 
demand. The Fly Ash Mission is doing extensive w ork on optimum flyash 
utilisation. The Government is also aware of the financial problems of the State 
Electricity Boards which is the other aspect referred to in the World Bank 
document. The Government has, consequently, focussed on the issue of reforms 
over the last two years. 
(b) No proposal has been received from the World Bank for conducting a 
study on India's power sector policies. 
(c) Does not arise. 
(d) and (e) The World Bank does not issue any guidelines in regard to 
India's power sector policies. They generally lay down covenants at the time of 
138 

[ 15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
signing the loan agreements with the operating/project implementing agencies 
for grant of loan for a particular power project/scheme. The Bank has its own 
internal operational procedures, policies and guidelines.

are due to pilferage; and

141 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2000] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The figures of tran smission arid 
distribution losses for the year 1998-99 are not yet available. According to the 
figures reported by SEBs/EDs/ Power Utilities, the T&D losses during the year 
1996-97 and 1997-98 on all India basis were 24.53% and 24.44% (tentative) 
respectively. However, the States which have undertaken restructuring have 
reported T&D losses varying from 40 to 51%. 
(d) The losses can be classified under two broad categories, namely, 
technical loss and commercial loss. The technical losses are inherent in the 
system and can be reduced by better design of lines, relocation of distribution 
transformers and installation of capacitors. The commercial losses are due to 
theft of energy, use of defective meters and unmetered supply. The losses due to 
theft and pilferage are presently, camouflaged under T&D losses. 
(e) In order to reduce the transmission & distribution losses, the Central 
Electricity Authority has issued comprehensive guidelines in July 1991, which, 
inter-alia provide for the following; 
 
— Up gradation of operating voltages; 
— Reducation of length of LT lines; 
— Location of transformers near load centres; 
— Adoption of low capacity transformers near consumers' pre- mises; 
— Installation of shunt capacitors; 
— Improvement in construction and operation techniques; and 
— Systematic and methodological approach for planning and design of 
distribution system on a long term basis. 
— Conducting energy audit and providing a methodology for segregating 
technical and commercial losses. 
Necessary amendments have been made in the Indian Elec tricity Act, 
1910, to make the theft of electricity a cognizable offence. 
Under the Accelerated Power Development Programme, it is proposed to 
provide funds to the State Governments for implement- ing specific projects for 
improving the sub-transmission and distribu- tion system including installation 
of state-of-the-art electronic meter- ing system. 
In the Conference of Power Ministers' which was held on 26.2.2000, the 
State/UT Governments have resolved to undertake energy auditing at all levels

and to install meters for all consumers by December, 2001. With the adoption of 
these measures, it will be possible to substantially reduce losses arising due to 
power thefts. 
Water and Air Pollution by Talcher Thermal Power Station 
2250. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that inhabitants of Talcher are suffering from various 
chest diseases due to the water and air pollution caused by Talcher Thermal 
Power Station; and 
(b) whether NTPC has any action plan to check this pollution? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) 
has the following two thermal power stations in Talcher area in Orissa:—  
1. Talcher Super Thermal Power Station (2500 MW) (TSTPS) which is 
under operation since 1995; and 
2. Talcher Thermal Power Station at Angul (460 MW 2110 MW) (TTPS) 
taken over by NTPC from Orissa State Electricity Board in June, 1995. 
No specific cases of sufferi ng from chest disease is reported due to air/ 
water pollution in areas where these stations are located. NTPC have taken 
various pollution control measures in TSTPS like provid - ing Electrostatic 
Precipitators (ESP) with 99.91 % efficiency, Stack of 275 meter height to control 
SOx and NOx level, providing closed loop cooling water system for thermal 
pollution control, dust extrac- tion and dust suppression system in coal handling 
plant/coal stack yard, providing fully automatic neutralisation system for DM 
Plant effluent, and Sewage Treatment Plant for treatment of township and plant 
sewage, providing Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations at different locations 
to contain air quality etc. Further, Multi Lagoon ash pond with zero discharge 
is under operation in the area. Ecological Impact Monitoring is being done by 
NTPC through M/s National Remote Sensing Agency. 
In regard to TTPS, immediately after taking over, NTPC took several 
steps in Stage-I units like repair of Air preheaters/soot blowers, chemical cleaning 
of Unit 1 and 2 and flue gas reconditioning which reduced the stack emission 
in Stage-I to 350-400 mg/NM3. NPTC has since finalised order on BHEL for 
retrofitting of additional ESPs in Stage -I Units. Additional ESPs have been 
retrofitted in Unit 5 and 6 of Stage-II units. The stack emission of these units is 
143 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2000] 
now well within the statutory limit of 150 mg/NM3. Direct flow of ash slury 
into Nandira river was stopped. Presently, Ash Pond Lagoon II is being used. 
Order for Sewerage Treatment Plant has been placed by NTPC. Order for ash 
water recirculation system is likely to be placed by April, 2000.

awarded for carrying out certain jobs, contractor deployes the requisite workmen

2279. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be

174

Incident of Caste Violence in Kolar District 
of Karnataka on 11th March, 2000 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): Sir, 
yesterday in this House a mention was made of the violent incidents in Kolar 
district of Karnataka. In that connection, it was stated that the Home Ministry 
should obtain the facts and come to the House. We ascertained the facts from 
the State Government and on that basis I make the following statement. 
As per information available with the Central Government, two 
incidents of violence and counter -violence between members of the Reddy 
community and the Scheduled Castes have been taken place in village 
Kambalapalli of Police Station Kencharlahaili in the District of Kolar, 
Karnataka. The incidents resulted in the stabbing  and subsequent death of 
one Krishna Reddy and burning alive of seven members of the Scheduled 
Caste community. 
The sequence of events reveals that on 11th March around 7.30 P.M. 
a group of 15-20 persons belonging to the Scheduled Caste community which. 
191 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2000] 
reportedly included two persons named Anjanappa and Sriramappa, stabbed 
one Krishna Reddy who died on the spot. In retaliation a group of 150 -200 
persons belonging to the Reddy community attacked the colony of the village 
inhabited by the Scheduled Caste community around 9.00 P.M. and set fire to 
the house belonging to Sriramappa and another adjoining house. Six persons, 
four men and two women, died on the spot due to suffocation and burn 
injuries and one lady succumbed to her injuries later on the way to hospital. 
The immediate provocation for the murder of Krishna Reddy is 
reported to be a verbal altercation between the Reddys and the Scheduled 
Castes on 9th March on some trivial issue. 
The State Police have arrested 15 pers ons in connection with the 
violence so far. Additional police force has also been stationed at the village 
as well as at the Divisional Headquarters at Chintamani and at District 
Headquarters, Kolar. Prohibitory orders have been enforced at Chintamani 
and Kambalapalli areas since 13th March, 2000. Investigations are on and 
senior police officials are supervising the investigation. The State Chief 
Minister, the State Home Minister and other leaders have visited the spot and 
assured protection to the remainin g Scheduled Caste families and arranged 
relief operations. The Chief Minister has announced institution of a judicial 
inquiry into the incident. The Chief Minister has also announced ex gratia 
compensation of Rs. 1 lakh to each, suitable employment to the next of kin of 
those killed, rehabilitation of the affected people and assured stringent action 
against those who were responsible for the heinous crimes. 
The situation is currently reported to be tense but under control. MR.

Non-Availability of Crop Loans in Orissa 
SHRI SANATAN BISI (Orissa): Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir. The 
non-availability of crop loans in Orissa is a serious matter. The poor 
cultivators in Orissa are suffering from untold miseries due to non -availability 
of crop loans in time. The commercial banks, including the State Bank of 
India, have not released the crop loans to cultivators although they were 
assured by bank officials on several occasions. The cultivators were expecting 
long-term loans from banks due to the super-cyclone in Orissa but to no avail. 
The issue of Kisan Credit Cards is also not satisfactory. I urge upon the 
Central Government to conduct a high -level inquiry regarding the non -
availability of crop loans in Orissa and to grant early relief to the cultivators.  
Thank you, Sir.

Urgent Need for Transit Facilities for North-East States Through 
Bangladesh, the Area Beinga Landlocked Region 
SHRI KHAGEN DAS (Tripura) : Mr. Vice -Chairman, Sir, I thank 
you for giving me an oppor tunity to raise the important issue of transit 
facilities to the land-locked North-East through Bangladesh for transportation 
of goods, materials and passengers. 
It is well known that even after 52 years of Independence, the 
North-East remains vulnerably p laced in terms of communication facilities. 
The entire North -East has to depend on just a small corridor through Assam 
which is called the Chicken's neck. The failure in developing appropriate 
transport and communication routes to the North -East is one of the most 
important reasons behind this region's under -development. Although the 
North-East region has a very large stock of oil and natural gas and other 
industrial raw materials, it has not been possible to utilise these natural 
resources for setting up o f industries, due to the transportation problems -  a 
halting hurdle for economic progress. 
It may be mentioned that before the partition of India, trade, traffic 
movement and communication of most of the North-East were linked with the 
plain lands of Briti sh India, now in Bangladesh. Immediately after 
Independence and partition of the country the traditional communication link 
through Bangladesh got snapped. 
I will specifically like to mention about the difficulties people have 
to face in my own State Tripura due to communication problems. 
The distance between Agartala and Calcutta through Bangladesh is 
not more than 400 kms. through the surface route. The aerial distance 
between Agartala and Calcutta is 350 kms. Compared to this, the rail -cum-
road distance from Agartala to Calcutta through Assam is 1,500 kms. The 
present rail -cum-road route passes through jungles, and many times, due to 
heavy rains, this route is blocked. 
It is against this background that the North- Eastern States have been 
requesting the Go vernment of India to take up this matter with the 
Government of Bangladesh so that transit facilities for Indian goods and 
passengers through Bangladesh could be available. The Chief Ministers of the 
North-Eastern States in a meeting at Guwahati last year also raised the 
demand.   A large section of Bangladesh trade community and intellectuals 
212 

[ 15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
favour the extension of the transit facility and direct communication with the 
North-Eastern States. There were series of exchanges  of visits of trade 
delegations and cultural teams from the North -Eastern States and Bangladesh 
during the last three years. Hence, there is the crying need of transit facility 
through Bangladesh for all the States in the North-Eastern region. 
It may be me ntioned that the Tripura Legislative Assembly has 
unanimously passed a Resolution in its last session, urging the Central 
Government to quicken the talks with Dhaka for a transit route through 
Bangladesh. 
The direct bus service between Dhaka and Calcutta i s a milestone in 
improving the bilateral relations between India and Bangladesh. The opening 
of the direct bus service between Calcutta and Dhaka raises a ray of hope for 
a similar facility in the minds of the people of the North -Eastern region, 
particularly Tripura. The people of Tripura and all other North -Eastern States 
expect and hope that the opening of the bus service, a transit route from 
Agartala to Calcutta via Bangladesh will soon materialise, with the initiative 
of the Government of India and co- operation of the Government of 
Bangladesh, in the interest of the economic development of the region as well 
as mutual benefit of the people of the subcontinent as a whole. 
Thank you, Sir. 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT 
SINGH): Sir, with your permission, I want to say that I am in sympathy with 
this requirement and demand. As the hon. Member already knows, this 
Government has already acted in this regard. After all, the opening of the 
land route between Calcutta and Dhaka and the bus journey is the first step 
that was taken for opening up trade transit through Bangladesh. We are in 
negotiation with the Bangladesh Government in this regard. 
The second aspect of the land route, as the hon. Member, no doubt, 
knows, is that we have already an agr eement, in principle, on connecting 
Dhaka with Agartala, through a bypass. That has also been agreed to. It is 
only a small portion of the road track, the road near Akhaura that has fallen 
into disuse. We have very purposely tried to have that restored. We have also 
spoken to the Government of Bangladesh. It is not simply about the land 
route. The agreement in principle is for a multi -model transport arrangement. 
These are the steps in that direction. I can assure you that the Government is 
already acting in this regard.

Service Rules For Lady Pilots of Indian Airlines 
PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY (West Bengal): Mr. Vice -
Chairman, Sir, I thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak. Sir, despite 
the constitutional provision of equality, irrespective of caste, class and gender, 
we see inequalities in these three areas. Therefore, Sir, I wish to draw the 
attention of the House to a case of gender discrimination in our own Indian 
Airlines. Sir, we are proud of our lady pilots and the Indian Airlines also 
declare that they are proud of their lady pilots. They employ the maximum 
number of lady pilots among all the commercial Airlines. But Sir, there are no 
service rules for lady pilots. Of course, they are granted maternity leave. But I 
understand that as soon as pregnancy in them is detected, they are not 
allowed to fly, and what is more, they are given leave without pay. Sir, 
pregnancy is not an offence, at least, it is not an offence according to the law 
of the land, it is not a disease, it is a natural condition, natural to womanhood. 
To penalise her for being pregnant is a case of blatant gender discrimination. 
Why should the lady pilot suffer financially because of pregnancy? If the 
medical authorities opine against the lady pilot flying during pregnancy, they 
should be given some ground jobs, and that too, in accordance with their 
grades. Their seniority must not suffer because of this change in their nature 
of work. At least up to two children, they should be given this faci lity and 
they must not suffer either financial loss or loss of seniority on account of 
pregnancy. I request the hon. Minister of Civil Aviation to instruct the Indian 
Airlines to frame appropriate service rules for the lady pilots.

[ 15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
STATUTORY RESOLUTION 
I. Seeking     Disapproval     of the  Telecom   Regulatory 
Authority of India (Amendment) Ordinance, 2000. 
II. The    Telecom     Regulatory    Authority    of    India 
(Amendment) Bill,, 2000. 
SHRI BALWANT SINGH RAMOOWALIA (Uttar Pradesh): Sir, I 
move that: 
'that this House disapproves of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of 
India (Amendment) Ordinance, 2000 (No.2 of 2000) promulgated by 
the President on the 24th January, 2000.' 
Sir, I speak with great anguish that the TRAI Ordinance was 
promulgated in utmost haste. One fails to understand, when there was a 
period of just three weeks or four weeks, an d Parliament was to be called, 
when both the Houses were to meet, why such an undue haste was shown, or 
why this step was taken. Sir, there are a few questions which demand 
immediate answer from the Government of India. The Ordinance was 
promulgated to rem ove the existing TRAI. Sir, a long time has passed and 
the Government has failed even to appoint all members for the TRAI. A few 
members were appointed, but not all. Now, Sir, I am quoting from Tribune, 
an English daily from Chandigarh : "The throttling mo nopoly of the DoT and 
the MTNL in two metropolitan cities and finally, the enthusiasm of the 
bureaucrats to retain their horses in power, India's tryst with wrong number is 
going to be long." 
Though MNCs have supported the Ordinance, by and large, the 
common users have not supported it. The overhauling of TRAI should have 
been done after adequate discussions. Sir, no time has been given to the 
representatives of the people, who are sitting here, to discuss the functioning 
of TRAI, its drawbacks and the need  for its further improvement. For 
instance, a serious doubt is prevailing in the mind of the common, man. We 
are aware of the functioning of the Government. All  important opinion-
makers have given their views. They say that when the session was just three  
weeks away, the Government should not have issued such an Ordinance. 
Obviously, there was pressure from certain quarters. What were the 
compulsions before the Government? Which were the lobbies involved in it 
which compelled the Government to take such a hasty decision? 
229 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2000] 
The country wants to know it. The Government must come out in 
the open. The loss of revenue suffered by the Government amounts to Rs.300 
crores. The Government has suffered this loss because they had deci ded to do 
away with the licence fee and to go in for revenue sharing. These things 
should have been discussed in the House. Through this Ordinance the 
Government has removed TRAI from the purview of C&AG. This is a very 
serious matter because C&AG has not taken a suo motu decision. The C&AG 
has thoroughly checked and investigated and has gone deeply into the 
functioning of the staff of TRAI. The C&AG has made a severe indictment 
of lavish expenditure by the members of TRAI during their trips abroad. It is 
very strange. Instead of controlling the lavish expenditure, the Government 
has unbridled them and has given them a free hand. These are the drawbacks. 
The Government will have to answer this question. Why have they done it? 
So far as modalities are concern ed, the Government has kept in mind only the 
views of the strongest lobby and the interested lobby. Where was the need for 
such a hurry? The Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Telecommunications was discussing this issue. Discussions were in progress. 
Meetings were going on and witnesses had been called to respond to the 
queries of the Members of the Committee. But the Government has 
completely bypassed and ignored the Standing Committee. Sir, this House 
cannot approve or accept this attitude of bypassing the Standing Committee. 
So, Sir, this House was not expecting any such ordinance. 
Ordinances are issued only when there is an utmost need or an emergency to 
meet some such issues which need immediate attention of the country and 
which are of very grave nat ure in larger interests of larger sections of the 
people. I do not want to use harsh words because of my respect for Shri 
Paswanji. But, as one of the great leaders, he has to explain why the 
Government had gone in for issuing an ordinance just for the benefit of some -
multinational companies. Sir, this House was expecting a full -fledged Bill on 
TRAI and not an ordinance. 
With these few words, I strongly oppose the ordinance and I urge 
upon the Minister that this ordinance be withdrawn, and that the right a nd 
supremacy of the House in discussing utmost, urgent matters in the House be 
restored and recognised. 
Thank you, Sir.

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI MD. SALIM): We will discuss the 
Statutory Resolution and the TRAI Bill together. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SANATAN BISI) in the Chair] 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL (Bihar): Mr. Vice -Chairman Sir, I am thankful 
to you for allowing me to participate in this discussion. I have listened very 
attentively to whatever the hon. Minister has stated on the floor of this House. 
I do not think there can be two opinions on the fact that in the modern world 
India must compete and unless there is quick progress in the area of 
telecommunications, we will certainly lag behind in certain core sectors 
which are necessary for our development. Having said that, Sir, I was a little 
pained to hear the Minister when he said, the purpose of a mending the 
original Act was to strengthen the TRAI. Whatever the hon. Minister said that 
the purpose of these amendments was indeed to strengthen the TRAI and that 
there was no ulterior purpose whatsoever. I am pained to hear that, 
237 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2000] 
because, if you look at the amendments and if you analyse the amendments 
one by one, you will realise that the primacy given to the TRAI in the original 
Act has been completely destroyed. 
From an independent authority functioning with transparency, it has 
become a dependent authority functioning under the control of the 
Government. That has been the effect of this amendment. I would request the 
hon. Minister to consider what I say very carefully. I will divide my address 
into three specific secti ons to prove my point. The first I take is of the 
composition and the constitution of the TRAI as envisaged under the 
amendment as opposed to the constitution and composition that was 
originally incorporated under the TRAI Act. 
Sir, as you know, originally, the TRAI was to consist of not less than 
two persons and not more than six persons. Secondly, originally, no member 
of the TRAI could be removed from his positron on account of certain 
specific provisions, for example, if a person has acquired financial or other 
interest as is likely to affect prejudicially his functions as a member, or has so 
abused his position as to render his continuance in office prejudicial to the 
public interest. These are clauses (d) and (e) of Section 7 of the original Act. 
Under the original Act, no member of the TRAI could be removed unless 
there was a reference in the Supreme Court, unless there was an inquiry held 
by the Supreme Court and in an answer to the reference the Supreme Court 
has advised that, in fact, that particula r person has acquired an interest or has 
abused his position. What has the new Act done, Sir? The new Act has 
removed that protection. Under the new Act, today, Sir, a member of the 
TRAI is nothing except a Government servant. I will demonstrate it to you 
presently, Sir. 
Section 7(2) says, No such person shall be removed from his office" 
under clause (d) and (e), which I read, of sub -section-(1), "unless he has been 
given a reasonable opportunity of being heard in the matter." Under the 
previous Section 7, there had to be an inquiry conducted by the Supreme 
Court, on a reference and only if the Supreme Court had decided that such 
person had abused his position, could such a person be removed but now you 
have removed that protection! Now you say under the new Act that he will be 
removed after giving him a reasonable opportunity which is available to every 
Government servant in this country. 
238 

[ 15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
So, instead of the primacy that the TRAI enjoyed under the original 
Act, you have, in fact, destroyed that primacy. You have made him dependent 
on the Government. That is point No.l. Now, point No.2. Originally such a 
person who was to be appointed as the Chairman of the TRAI had to be either 
a Judge of the Supreme Court, retired or sitting , a Chief Justice of the High 
Court, retired or sitting. You have also removed that provision. Now you say 
you will appoint him, provided he is familiar with the area, he has special 
knowledge in telecommunication, industry, finance, accountancy, law and 
other things. Therefore, instead of having a judicial officer as the head of the 
TRAI, you will now have your own person. What is your intention? Why did 
you bring about these changes? Was the previous Chairman not listening to 
you? Is it not a fact that th e previous Chairman was being barraged, was being 
questioned by the DoT, when he exercised his functions? Is it not a fact that 
there was a case pending in the High Court wherein the DoT was challenging 
the authority of the TRAI? Is it not a fact that in t he High Court the TRAI 
went to a Division Bench of the Delhi High Court to say, "Please interpret the 
statute and decide what our functions are to be." Is this not a fact? What did 
you do? By one stroke of the pen, you removed all the appointees under the 
previous Act. And that is the reason for an Ordinance. You issued an 
Ordinance on 24th January because you knew that the Parliament was not in 
session. You incorporated a provision in that Ordinance which is now a part of 
this Bill wherein you said that all previous appointments are hereby done away 
with. So, overnight you removed them. Why? Because they were functioning 
independently, because they were discharging their functions transparently, 
and this was not to the liking of the Government. So much for your claim that 
you want to strengthen the TRAI. Now I come to the second point and that 
relates to powers and functions of the TRAI. You look at the previous Act. I 
was amazed when I was comparing the powers and functions under the 
previous Act which are now set out in section 11 of the new Bill and what I 
found was rather interesting. Under the previous Act, the TRAI, in fact, had 
the authority to recommend the terms and conditions of the licence and also 
revoke the licence of a subscriber or any service provider. Now what you 
have cleverly done is that you have divided the functions of the TRAI into 
recommendatory functions and other functions. You have included the 
revocation of the licence under recommendatory functions. In other words, if 
the TRAI found under the original Act that a particular service provider was 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2000] 
violating the conditions of licence or doing things which were not in public 
interest, the TRAI could, in fact, recommend or decide on the revocation of 
the licence. Now the TRAI considered the MTNL also as a service provider. 
Where is the hub of the problem? The problem is that the MTNL is as much 
a service provider as any other private entity is. So, the TRAI considered 
both these service providers at par, level playing field that you talk about. 
Now, when you realised that the TRAI in exercise of its powers acted against 
the MTNL, the DoT did not want that. So, what did the Government do? The 
Government decided that as far as the Government is concerned, it  is above 
the TRAI, as far as the DoT is concerned it is above the TRAI. 
It is the licensor, which is why you have included the definition of 
licensor, for the first time, in this amendment Bill. And, because it is the 
licensor and because it is above the TRAI, now, the TRAI cannot act against 
the MTNL at all. Now, it is a part of its powers on recommendations. It is for 
the Government to accept that recommendation or not. The entire structure of 
the TRAI Bill, which caters to independence, which caters to transparency, 
which caters to a level -playing field amongst all the service providers, you 
have destroyed it by one stroke of a pen. Is this how you wanted to strengthen 
the TRAI? I give you yet another example. There were two very important 
powers in the original Act which vested with the TRAI. One was to protect 
the interests of the consumers of telecommunication services. It was a very 
wide power. The TRAI could issue any direction, do anything to protect the 
interests of the service providers. It was ta ken out. That power now does not

disputes between the service providers, it would mean that if there is a dispute

out. No such power exists in the present Bill. Why? Because the TRAI

Court. And how many years does it take in the Supreme Court? So, you have 
changed the whole process.

sufficient powers and with certain safeguards, within the main body of TRAI is very 
necessary. In a consumer society the big people have the wherewithal to take care 
of their interests. But if there is no in -built provision within the regulator itself 
for securing and safeguarding the interests of the small users, it will be a great 
disservice to the national and social objectives which you are espousing in the 
Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill. 
Sir, I do not want to make it acrimonious. Let the Gov ernment 
exercise its mind. There is no sense of victory or defeat in this matter. Let us go 
back to the Standing Committee. Let us have a proper review because this is very 
crucial. Finally, I would say that the way in which we have evolved the telecom 
regulator, is going to influence the functioning of so many other parameters which 
will come into play in the entire gamut of this industry.

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): Sir, 
I beg to move:

RAJYA SABHA 115 March, 2000] 
"That the Bill further to amend the Recovery of Debts due to 
Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, as passed by 
Lok Sabha, be taken into consideration." Mr. Vice- Chairman, Sir, as 
the hon. Members are aware, the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and 
Financial Institutions Act, 1993 was enacted on August 27, 1993 to provide 
for establishment of tribunals for expeditious adjudication and recovery of 
debts due to banks and financial ins titutions and for matters connected 
therewith, or, incidental thereto. To implement the provisions of the above 
Act, action was initiated for establishment of ten recovery tribunals and one 
appellate tribunal in the country. Subsequently, four more Appella te 
Tribunals and five more DRTs were sanctioned. Some of them have already 
been set up, while the remaining are in the process of being set up. Further, I 
wish to inform this august House that Delhi the High Court Bar Association 
filed a writ petition in t he High Court of Delhi in July, 1994 challenging the 
validity of the DRT Act. The High Court, in its judgement, dated 10.3.95, had 
declared the Act as unconstitutional and void. Government filed a special writ 
petition in the Supreme Court and the order of  the Delhi High Court was 
stayed. During the hearing of the case before the Supreme Court, certain 
observations, which, inter alia, included maintainability of counter -claim, set 
off, and reconstitution of the Selection Committee were made, which were 
considered by the Government. Based on the observations of the hon. High 
Court and suggestions of the Working Groups set up by the RBI and the Rajya 
Sabha Committee on Subordinate Legislation, the Act has been amended 
suitably through an Ordinance, dated 17.1. 2000. The main provisions of the 
Bill relate to maintainability of set off and counter -claim, appointment of 
additional Recovery Officers, transfer of cases from one DRT to another. 
This Bill seeks to replace the said Ordinance of 17.1.2000. 
Sir, yesterday this House spent the whole day discussing the question of 
NPAs of banks with which this legislation is supposed to deal. We had very 
extensive discussions and I would, therefore, recommend, Sir, that we can 
take up this Bill for consideration, and if poss ible, pass it without discussion 
today.

SHRI VAYALAR RAVI (Kerala): Sir, there is no dispute over the 
Bill because this Bill has  come before the House after it had been seriously 
considered by the Committee of this House. It is based on the judgement of 
the Supreme Court. The whole House is in support of this measure of the 
Government which is related to debt relief and speedy reco very of debts. I 
agree with the hon. Finance Minister that we had an elaborate and detailed 
discussion, a day ago, regarding the NPAs. The Government also made its 
position clear on certain aspects. I have no dispute over many of the aspects 
which the hon. Minister had mentioned, such as secrecy and the international 
banking system. Sir, no Government can open to everybody the accounts of 
every bank. It is not possible. It is against the very tenets of the international 
law, and also the banking system has its own secrecy. So, 1 appreciate the 
Government's position. The only point I want to make is this. The hon. 
Minister has put it in a nice fashion that we are not reducing the powers of the 
nationalised bank; our capital in the bank will remain as it is. a nd we will 
make more capital formation by selling more shares, and in that process we 
may reduce to 30%. This is what the hon. Minister has said. But this is not a 
point which has to be debated now. When the hon. Minister said this thing 
yesterday, I stood up to express my reservation to that observation. Sir. the 
hon. Minister also will agree with me that the nationalisation of banks has 
generated so much of enthusiasm among the people. Sir, even the banks can 
go to the villages. As it stands today, the nu mber of branches of the banks is 
about 60,000, though some banks are running under loss. The household 
savings have also gone more to the banks. We also said the same thing at the 
time of the discussion on the Bill  on Insurance. Because the household 
savings have gone to the banks, their capital has gone up to three -lakh crores 
of rupees. Sir, I know every bank, including the nationalised banks as well as 
the private banks work under the supervision and guidance of the Reserve 
Bank. No bank can violate the guidelines of the Reserve Bank. You are 
intervening in that matter also. This is an in -built system and no Government 
can manipulate in that system. These banks which have the money power are 
the nationalised banks, and it gives you the leverage to control  the economy 
for the benefit of the nation. Suppose there is inflation and the money supply 
increases; and in these types of situations, these nationalised banks give a 
leverage to keep the economy under control, and as a result, the Government 
can do better in these situations.

RAJYA SABHA [ 15 March, 2000] 
So, Sir, when the holdings of the Government come down to 30 per 
cent, it means that the control will go to private hands. The Government leverage 
will come down. It may create problems. 
I agree with the hon. Minister that some banks are making losses. I will 
give you one example. I have not much time. One bank-I think it is a Calcutta 
based bank-has a branch in Karukutty. That was opened for a factory called the 
"Premier Cable." That has been closed. The bank branch still remains there. This 
branch can go to another town, Ankamali. This is only an example. The Reserve 
Bank says, "No. You function here." There is no transaction at all. Ten 
members of its staff are sitting in that branch. The Reserve Bank does not allow it 
to go to another small town to function there. How can you blame the bank for 
this loss because ten persons are sitting there without any transaction? Therefore, 
this kind of a bureaucratic approach in this sector is not correct. 
The other point is about the commercial activities of banks. The 
commercial activities of banks should be encouraged. They want to bring them 
under the control of the CAG. I do not agree with that. They were never 
brought under the purview of the CAG because these are commercial activities. I do 
not agree with their perception that the CAG should look into all these things. The 
Congress Government followed that policy, and you are following it. I have no 
quarrel with that. 
Without taking much time, I am suggesting one thing to the hon. Minister. 
His Budget Speech has elaborately dealt with this subject. I want him to 
reconsider this. Do not leave the nationalised banks to the mercy of some other 
people. They are your own property. They give you so much of econo mic 
strength. 
The last point is that the nationalised banks have played an important role 
in the social sector, for the benefit of the downtrodden people. In every State, lead 
banks have been linked with the programmes you announced and even the 
Congress Government announced. They have done a good job to an extent. The 
recovery may be less. 
I can also tell you from my experience that no business house can make 
any complaint that it could not get any project processed because of the nationalised 
banks. Every project, whether it is for a big business or a medium business, 
has been processed with good speed.   They have been

assisted, helped. Maybe, the NPAs might have accumulated. However, the 
fact remains that the nationalised banks never stand in the way of big business 
or a medium business. Naturally, they will stand in the way of small people. 
They want all kinds of securities from them. They want all kinds of 
properties. They need securities even for a loan of Rs.l lakh. A s far as big 
business is concerned, there is no quarrel. They have always helped it. 
I conclude by saying that while supporting this measure, I will again 
appeal to the hon. Minister one thing. As he has reiterated  his position even 
yesterday, people like me have a little worry. We have some apprehension 
because any kind of dilution of the Government holdings in the nationalised 
banks will not help in the future. It will not help you as the Finance Minister. 
It is strength. It is an economic strength. It is strength in your hands. You can 
dictate terms to the people who try to play with the Indian economy. 
Consider this point well in time.

THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L. K. ADVANI): 
My Statement this morning refers to an invitation to air militant groups which 
are operating. It is not an invitation issued to each separately. It  is a public 
statement mady by the Prime Minister and the Government spokesman from 
time to time. I referred specifically to the first visit of the Prime Minister to 
the North-East during which he made a public statement that he would like all 
those groups who for various reasons have taken to militancy to come for a 
dialogue. Of course, in the course of the discussion, I would like to make it 
clear that any solution that can be brought about will be within the four 
corners of the Constitution. So, on this basis, we have been trying. Someone 
asked, 'Are you in touch with the underground?' They are all underground. 
What is their source of contact? I am sure anyone .who has been in the 
Government, who has faced this situation, is aware that a time comes when, 
for various reasons, if a particular group feels tha t what they are doing at the 
moment is not yielding results, then soundings take place. It is in the course 
of such soundings that we have had some kind of informal talks with the 
BLT. They responded. It is true that several Members referred to the fact that 
NDFB is not here. It is true. The Statement that I have made is about BLT. 
One thing that should be known about BLT is that this is an organisation 
which has sought Bodoland as a separate state, not as  a sovereign state, but 
within the Indian Union. 
288 

[ 15 March, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
But when they formed this BLT seven years back, they said that 
Bodoland will be formed not by petitions, prayers and democratic process, 
but by taking to arms and, therefor e, they became a militant organisation 
formally, saying that, "Our objective is to create a separate Bodoland State 
for the survival of the Bodos and to develop and organise insurgency and 
underground activities, leading to mass revolution for the creation  of a 
separate Bodoland State". Now, with this declared objective, we felt that 
when they approached the Government and said, "We are willing to talk to 
you in respect of a separate State of Bodoland; we are willing to abjure 
violence", we will say yes. No w, the kind of questions that have been raised 
by-several Members are very reasonable. I can tell you that the specific 
conditions that they have agreed to are three- fold. These are: (a) BLT will 
completely abjure the path of violence; (b) BLT will not eng age in violent or 
unlawful activities like killings, injuries, kidnappings, extortions, 
intimidation, "etc.; and, (c) - which is even more important, because it covers 
the whole gamut --  BLT agrees to abide by the Constitution of India and the 
laws of the land. Now, with these three commitments made by them, they 
say that, "We are willing to make these commitments, provided the 
Government says that it will not carry on its operations against the BLT". So, 
this has been done in consultation with the State Go vernment of Assam, 
namely, the Governor of Assam and the Chief Minister of Assam, who have 
been in the picture. So much so, that it was decided that when the Central 
Government apprises Parliament on this particular agreement, simultaneously, 
the Chief Min ister of Assam will apprise the State Assembly also of this 
agreement. So, this is somewhat different from what has been done earlier. 
The questions raised by hon. Swaraj Kaushal are very valid because when we 
came into office, there was an agreement enter ed into by the earlier 
Government with the NSCN (I -M) and we inherited that. Because of that 
agreement, there was a cease- fire in Nagaland. We considered the whole 
thing and we came to the conclusion that because there was a cease-fire, let us 
not do anything which disrupted the cease- fire; let us continue the cease- fire. 
A question was asked by Dhrupadji saying that, "In that case, you have not 
imposed the condition, "within the four parameters'; they also say that they 
want sovereignty and they want independence and yet you are discussing with 
them. Why can't you have the same approach about ULFA?" I said that that 
was not an agreement entered into by this Government, but we inherited it 
and we considered the pros and cons and came to the conclusion that -

although if we were there, we may not have done it and that we would have 
done it in this way; so, on that account —  let us not disrupt the cease -fire that 
is there; let us continue it; let us negotiate, though, in t he course of the 
discussion, we have made it clear to them that so far as the Government of 
India was concerned, the Government of India would like to find a solution to 
their problems within the four parameters of the Constitution of India. This 
has been made clear in the course of negotiations. In case fresh and new 
negotiations are to be started, we would like to make it clear to the militant 
groups right from the outset. Similarly, there was the other question about the 
area, etc. In this case, basicall y, it is the area within Assam where the 
autonomous council is sought to be set up. 
Though, at this point of time, I would not say that these things have 
been put down in black and white, basically, when they agreed to abide by the 
Constitution and the law s of the land, I think the BLT should be depended 
upon to carry on the negotiations properly. I think something good will come 
of it. We would be happy if the other groups also decided in a similar way to 
abjure violence, accept the Constitution of India, the laws of the land and 
come to discuss with us. But if the others don't, there is no reason why we 
should not talk to a group that has offered. And mind you, it may be a smaller 
group than the NDFT, but I find, in the last few years, the kind of casualti es 
inflicted on the people, on the security forces, are not minor. They have also 
lost their lives; they have been arrested in large numbers; they have 
surrendered. The numbers that are attributable to the Bodo Liberation Tigers 
do indicate that there is a hard core of activists in that organisation and if they 
come to the mainstream, it is for the good of Assam, and good of the country. 
Therefore, the Government has accepted this. 
Santoshji was taking exception to my observations that there are 
positive re sponses. In situations of this kind, I can only say that positive 
responses mean, direction is for the good. I would never claim that militancy 
has been contained in Assam. No, I would not say that. But I find that they 
are losing support; this time, they called for a boycott of the elections, but the 
poll percentage was over 70. This is one index. Similarly, when you have half-
a-dozen or ten incidents happening in the countryside where the ULFA 
extremists are surrounded by the villagers, they are lynched b y the villagers, 
they are handed over to the police; they are evidences that things are moving 
in a positive direction. I am not citing the figures and statistics which show 
that in the last two years, things have been gradually coming down and down

and down, though, of course, when an incident of the kind that took place in the 
last week of February occurs, when a Minister was killed, it certainly creates a 
news; it may strengthen the morale of the extremists and demora lises the 
common man, but that does not mean that the basic fact is wrong. This kind of an 
incident - a landmine explosion -- it can happen. I would not rule it out, but the 
facts which are with us, and which I have presented to Parliament earlier also, 
do indicate that with the combined efforts of the State Government; the police 
there; the para-military forces; and to some extent, the Army also, militancy is 
being contained. They have lost the support of the people considerably, which 
is a great achievement. Therefore, in the North-East, on the whole, the evidences 
are positive. Thank you, Sir.

what has happened in Kambalapalli village in Karnataka, I am really ashamed of it. 
It is not a simple local law and order problem. It is not an isolated incident. 
Tension has been brewing in that area for the last two or three years. In 1997, five 
people were killed. In 1998, five people were killed in the Chinthamani taluk. This 
village comes under Chinthamani taluk which is bordering die State of Andhra 
Pradesh. As Shri Hanumanthappa has said, this has got a larger perspective; the 
growing assertion and consciousness among the weaker sections on the one side; 
and, on die other die inability of die other people to u nderstand and digest this 
assertion. Sir, if you see here, these people, Dalits, who met die Chief Minister on 
his arrival in die village, said, "Others will get angry if we wear shoes, trousers and 
shirts."

Even after 50 years, this is the situation! Even if it is the feeling —
whether it is true or not —really, one should think about it very seriously. 
The entire country and the society should think about it. There is need for 
social awareness on this count. 
Secondly, here the village Dalit Sriramappa, who has been killed, 
contested the Sarpanch election. The others thought, "This fellow could 
come to this level and contest the election in the village!". This is another 
provocation for that. The third thing is the local inci dent. My point is, I do 
not want to give it any political colour. I do not think any politics is involved. 
It may be local panchayat politics. But the fact of the matter is, the Home 
Minister's statement as it was given to the House, is totally a report, a  simple 
report, given by the Government of Karnataka. I am sorry to say that this 
report is not at all a comprehensive report and this is not giving the true picture 
of what exactly has happened, what the background is and what action the 
local administration there has taken. I have the information that the police who 
was in the village after the Friday's incident was withdrawn from the village 
just one hour before this incident. What is the reason? How can anybody give 
an explanation? There were incidents earlier; there was tension earlier; there 
were caste clashes going on. We are not here to blame a particular 
community, this community or that community. We have our sympathy for 
the Dalits. But, at the same time, it is the duty of a civilised government, duty 
of the administration, duty of the police, to give the needed protection, 
particularly, in view of the growing tension between the communities there 
and the past incidents also. But, we do not know why the police was 
withdrawn. 
One more astonishing thing is that the mob which set fire to the 
houses stopped the fire -fighting force personnel from entering the village for 
more than half an hour, resulting in the death of two more persons. They 
could have been saved. I am no t quoting from anything. This is  a newspaper 
report which appeared in the Deccan Herald and the Indian Express. And my 
own party people who had gone there as a fact -finding team, had also come 
to the conclusion that it was callousness on the part of the administration 
there locally which had resulted in this ghastly incident. Otherwise, it would 
not have happened. As I told you, it is not an isolated incident. Other 
Members also said there were earlier instances. Krishna Reddy was 
murdered. We condemn the murder. Action has to be taken ag ainst those 
people. But what is it that the administration has done in view

of the sensitivity of the situation? There is no explanation from the 
Government. I cannot expect the Home Minister to answer on behalf of the 
State Government. I do not want him to get involved in this controversy also. 
As a Member of this House representing Karnataka, as a person 
representing a political party, I want to share my anguish on the callous 
manner in which the entire thing has been dealt with. I do not want to go into 
other incidents now and take the time of the House. But the entire approach 
of the administration there was totally callous. There was a total failure on 
the part of the administration. So, 1 feel that simply ordering a j udicial 
inquiry now will not help. Judicial inquiry, we all know about. Unless people 
go to the judicial authorities and file affidavits and then are able to produce 
evidence, nothing will happen. Therefore, I suggest, instead of that, there 
should be an i nvestigating agency to find out, firstly, the persons who are 
responsible; secondly, the circumstances that have led to the incident; and, 
thirdly, the failure of the local administration. All these things should come 
out. Then only will it act as a warnin g to the other people. It will also stop 
further escalation of tension in other areas. That being the case, I demand that 
there should be a Central Bureau of Investigation inquiry. I know that the 
Centre cannot do it without the acceptance of the State Gov ernment. But 1 
appeal to the State Government, in their own interest, in the interest of the 
State, that they should also come forward to hand over this case to the CBI. 
The Dalit organisations in the entire district have observed a bandh' in 
Chintamani district. They also want to have a CBI inquiry into the incident. I 
request the Home Minister to communicate to the Karnataka Government the 
wish of the House. I believe that the entire House agrees with the suggestion. 
Cutting across party lines, we should really go tough on this matter so that it 
acts as a deterrent for the future. 
Then, I request the Home Minister to find out from the State 
Government what their rehabilitation plan is. The entire community has left 
the village. The entire community has left the village now. Peace is there now 
because people are not there in the village. What is their rehabilitation plan? 
How are you going to rehabilitate them? This also should be made known. I 
think, the Central Government, as suggested by Hanumanthappaji, and also 
the State Government from time to time, under the chairmanship of the Prime 
Minister or the Home Minister or the Chief Minister should have quarterly 
meetings to review this aspect of atrocities committed against the weaker 
sections and women. These are all vulnerable sections in our society.

SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI (Uttar Pradesh) : Sir, we are discussing 
a very tragic and ghastly incident. It becomes all the more shameful for each 
and every one of us that such incidents go on occuring again and again, 
despite the discussions that we have had many a time. I would like to first 
mention that I agree with the broad exposition, the broad approach and the 
thrust that Shri Hanumanthappa had given to this problem in general, in order 
to have a satisfactory and an enduring solution. There are a number of things, 
but, particularly, monitoring and better coordination between the various 
Ministries at the Centre and the State Governments is certainly called for. I 
would not like to go into this aspect any more, exce pt mentioning that, at one 
point of time, certainly, the Ministry of Home Affairs was responsible for 
looking after the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes. 
Sir, I would like to confine myself to just one or two clarifications. 
Firstly, it is true that the Home Minister's statement is, ~ as it is natural in our 
Constitutional set up - based on the information supplied by the State 
Governments. But, still, a little bit more of scrutiny of the information and a 
little more careful questioning of this in formation is certainly called for. In 
Para 3 it is mentioned that, 'The immediate provocation for the murder of

Whenever we hear of such incidents taking* place, we

always express our anguish. But many such incidents have taken place earlier also. 
This is not the only incident where people have been scorched to death. In my

happen, sometimes the Scheduled Castes are affected, sometimes people 
belonging to both the communities are affected. Whenever such incidents 
happen, we always talk of conducting investigations in a fa ir manner. 
Sometimes judicial inquiries are held. After that, charge-sheets are also sent to 
courts. But, how can we prevent such incidents? This has never been thought of. 
Our laws are such. I don't say that there are no penal laws in India. There is' the 
Indian Penal Code. There is the Prevention of Atrocities Against Scheduled Castes 
and Scheduled Tribes Act also. 
There is the Protection of Civil Rights Act. There are many penal laws. 
But, at the same time, the investigation in which the police is involv ed or the 
investigating authorities are involved, their investigation is not at all believed even 
today, as it is believed in the other countries. Therefore, there is a need to amend 
the Evidence Act and the Criminal Procedure Code so that the procedure of  
conducting the investigation, the investigation which has been conducted by 
honest people, or. by honest officers could be believed in the court, the accused 
could be convicted and there is no chance of the accused going scot -free. 
Therefore. I would like  to know whether the Government is thinking amending 
the Indian Evidence Act which was framed long before. I would also like to know 
whether the Government is thinking in terms of amending the Indian Penal Code 
and the Criminal Procedure Code so that proceedings in respect of such heinous 
crimes could be conducted, and the accused who have committed such offences 
could be punished.
